display.name: Marcus Rivera
display.blurb: A freelance designer, 38, with lumpy income: paid in USDC, a late client, a scam message and an exploited vault.

intro: Marcus Rivera, 38, freelance designer. His income is lumpy, so he keeps three ring-fenced pools: runway (emergency savings), tax, and optional (experiments). Business cash $2,400, personal checking $900, emergency savings $2,600, no crypto, no debt. A business credit card (limit $1,500, 2% a month) is unused.
plan: Stablecoin limit: hold no more than $1,500 in USDC at a time.
Runway: emergency savings target $6,000 (two months of personal spending). He has $2,600. Runway money is not for yield.

Tax reserve is committed money. It is for the next estimated payment, not for experiments. Real estimated-tax dates are April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15; this story uses a simplified schedule and an assumed set-aside rate.
Operating buffer: about $1,500 stays in business cash. Cash above it is surplus that can be moved.
Records: log every crypto receipt and every conversion.
Wallet safety: never sign an unsolicited request, and never pay a fee to "release" money.

questions.situation: A client pays a $2,500 invoice in USDC. In this story the invoice counts as $2,500 of income when you receive it, whether or not you convert it, so 20% of net receipts is set aside either way (a simplifying assumption in this scenario). USDC is a dollar stablecoin, not an insured deposit. You can convert it to dollars for a 1% fee.

a.t: Convert all of it to dollars.

c.t: Hold all of it in USDC.

Next: business cash is {x.b.BIZ-post.BIZ} lower than if you had converted half and {x.a.BIZ-post.BIZ} lower than if you had converted it all. That matters in Q4 if a client pays late.

questions.takeaway: A payment in crypto is still a payment you have to plan for. Decide how much you will hold before it arrives, and set the tax money aside either way.

questions.title: The client pays late
questions.disclosure: You are choosing a **standing plan** for months 6 and 7, not predicting this month's gap. The plan is scored on the order it puts your safety nets in: spend less or use your own emergency savings first, and a 2%-a-month card last. That is judged from what you hold now. It does not depend on whether a gap actually appears, and nothing later is used to score it.

questions.situation: A client delays a $3,200 payment. This month only **$2,400** arrives instead of $5,600. You normally move $3,000 from business cash to personal checking and spend $3,000. Whether your personal checking is short depends on how much cash the business has.

a.t: Keep spending $3,000. If personal checking runs short, cover the gap from emergency savings.

b.t: Cut personal spending to $2,200 a month for months 6 and 7.

c.t: Put any gap on the business credit card (2% a month) and leave emergency savings alone.

questions.takeaway: A late client tests cash flow. Use the runway or trim spending before borrowing at 2% a month, and notice that holding the invoice in USDC left the business with less cash exactly when it was needed.

questions.title: Sign here to release your invoice
questions.situation: A message appears to come from a client. It asks you either to **sign a wallet message** or to **pay a $45 "verification fee"** to "release" an invoice. You did not ask for it.

a.t: Ignore it and do not sign or pay.

questions.takeaway: Money is rarely "released" by signing or paying a stranger. When a request is unsolicited and urgent, verify it independently.

a.t: Withdraw what is left (if any) and rebuild emergency savings with business cash above $1,500.

c.t: Add $500 to Apex Yield to recoup.
